claims.text: A nitrite-based inhibitor adsorbs onto the pre-exposure surface of Q235 steel.
Inhibitor adsorption alters the surface chemical composition and forms a protective conversion film.
The nitrite-based film is stable at room temperature and 100 °C.
The conversion film occupies active corrosion sites.
The conversion film acts as a barrier between chloride ions and the metal surface.
Adsorption of the inhibitor changes the local electrochemical potential.
The adsorption-modified surface suppresses anodic dissolution.
Loss or desorption of the film at elevated temperature diminishes its protective effect.
The treatment suppresses corrosion initiation and propagation in chloride-rich environments at both room temperature and 100 °C.
Treated Q235 samples will exhibit lower corrosion current density than untreated samples.
Treated Q235 samples will exhibit delayed pitting initiation relative to untreated samples.
Treated Q235 samples will exhibit lower overall degradation rates than untreated samples.
Q235 steel in the as-received state has an intact native surface.
The controlled study compares nitrite-treated and untreated Q235 steel under otherwise identical conditions.
The test environment is 3.5 wt% NaCl at controlled relative humidity, evaluated at room temperature and 100 °C.
A stable treated film accompanied by corrosion current density comparable to or greater than the untreated reference would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis characterizes the film as temperature-stable through 100 °C, while the uncertainty field allows partial desorption or reorganization at elevated temperature.

Delayed pitting initiation is predicted as evidence of protection, but the falsification rule states that an increased pitting initiation time would falsify the hypothesis. An increased initiation time would normally support, not refute, the prediction.

The mechanism explicitly predicts diminished protection if the film degrades, yet film instability is also labeled a decisive falsification. Film degradation would violate the stated stability boundary condition rather than decisively refute adsorption-mediated protection by an intact film.
